newsitem.title: GERMANY: Yeltsin to fly home after talks on NATO with Kohl.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to fly home after talks on NATO with Kohl.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin flies home on Friday morning for a brief holiday after talks with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl that seemed to leave the door open to a settlement of Moscow's row with NATO over the alliance's eastward expansion.

Yeltsin, 66, looked pale and tired during a sunny day spent with Kohl, his personal friend and political ally, in the German spa resort of Baden-Baden. But he came away declaring optimism that their special relationship could unblock the snags and allow a signing date of May 27 date for a NATO-Russia treaty in Paris to go ahead.
But, while Yeltsin, who has had major heart surgery and pneumonia in the last five months takes a break, intensive negotiations will be needed to make that a "reality", a Kremlin spokesman said.

Yeltsin's spokesman said the president and his wife Naina may fly directly from Stuttgart (1000 GMT) to the Black Sea resort of Sochi for a few days holiday before returning to Moscow next week for talks with Chinese leader Jiang Zemin.

At a ceremony to accept a "Man of the Year" award from the German media on Thursday night, Yeltsin renewed his demand for a binding treaty giving Moscow guarantees that the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's expansion into eastern Europe would not threaten Russia's security.

He repeated his criticism that making former Soviet bloc states members of the western pact risked reopening divides in Europe after the efforts Russia had made to introduce democratic reforms and end the ideological conflict of the Cold War.

"Broadening military alliances, advancing NATO's military infrastructure towards Russia's borders, will not create a united peaceful Europe," Yeltsin said, reading his speech clearly but showing more signs of fatigue than in other recent appearances since he returned to work from illness two months ago.

Kohl told the gathering, in a stately health resort that once played host to tsars and Russia's 19th-century elite, that his "friend" Yeltsin's "trademark" was his refusal to shy away from any political confrontation.

Both men referred to Russian writer Fyodor Dostoevsky, whose 1860s novel "The Gambler" immortalised Baden-Baden and its casino. Yeltsin appeared to be gambling on Kohl's support to reach a deal with NATO by next month.

"We want to announce that...on the 27th of May in Paris an agreement will be signed by the leaders of the NATO countries and of Russia," Yeltsin told a news conference, before adding, "So we'll have to hurry".

"It was very important for me that Helmut Kohl supported Russia's line," Yeltsin said. "I am sure that such an authoritative politician as Helmut Kohl will exert his influence so that there will be objectivity in these issues."
Kohl said he hoped a deal on NATO could be struck next month with German help. But he noted the obstacles ahead.
Russia wants a binding agreement from NATO not to deploy new troops and weapons in new member states and is also seeking a say in the pact's decision-making.
NATO leaders, especially the United States, are unwilling to give in so far to Moscow that that would consign new members like Poland and Hungary to "second-class" NATO participation.
"I am confident that, with goodwill on both sides, we can come to an agreement before the NATO-Russia summit on May 27," Kohl said. "It still needs a lot of work but I see good chances."
Kohl and Yeltsin also said they had also made progress in settling a long dispute over German art treasures seized by the Soviet Army after World War Two.

There would be no quick solution but in a gesture of goodwill Yeltsin brought Kohl a collection of papers of the 1922 German foreign minister Walther Rathenau and announced he had ordered the release to Germany of copies of the East German communist party records held in Moscow since the 1970s.

They also aim to boost economic ties by setting up a new forum headed by both leaders and to promote Russia's membership of international economic organisations like the World Trade Organisation, the Group of Seven and the Paris Club of lenders.
